lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: understand how the small intestine is adapted for absorption, including the structure of a villus

primer.text: You know digestion ends with small soluble molecules, but absorption is its own engineering problem. This lesson shows how the small intestine solves it: length, folding and millions of villi — each villus a one-cell-thick pump with its own capillary network and lacteal, moving glucose, amino acids and fats into the body.

modules.title: Absorption: Routes into the Blood
modules.opening: Absorption carries the small digested molecules across from the gut into the blood and lymph: glucose and amino acids take the blood route, fatty acids and glycerol travel in the lymph. The crossings happen by diffusion, and sometimes by active transport, with water taken up by osmosis.
keyPoints: Absorption moves digested molecules from the gut into the blood and lymph.
Glucose and amino acids enter the blood; fatty acids and glycerol enter the lymph.
Absorption proceeds mainly by diffusion, sometimes by active transport.
Water is absorbed by osmosis, mostly in the small intestine.
The large intestine also absorbs water from the residue.

low.restatement: Small soluble molecules cross into blood and lymph; water follows by osmosis.
low.analogy: Freight crossing a border by two routes — road (blood) and rail (lymph).
low.examPointer: Pair each product with its route; the pairing earns the mark.

medium.restatement: Active transport tops up absorption when diffusion alone would leave valuable molecules behind.
medium.analogy: A pay-to-enter lane alongside the free one.
medium.examPointer: Name the transport mechanisms: diffusion, active transport, osmosis for water.

modules.title: Villi: The Absorption Machinery
sourceHeadings: The role of villi in the small intestine
modules.opening: The small intestine is long, folded and studded with millions of villi — finger-like projections that multiply its absorbing surface enormously. Each villus is one cell thick, so diffusion stays short; microvilli roughen its surface further; and inside, blood capillaries plus a lacteal sweep the absorbed products away, keeping the gradient steep.
keyPoints: The intestine's length and folding raise its absorbing surface massively.
Villi are tiny finger-like projections numbering in the millions.
Microvilli on each villus enlarge the surface further.
A villus wall is one cell thick, minimising the diffusion distance.
Blood capillaries carry glucose and amino acids away; a lacteal carries fats.
Enzymes in the villus walls aid the final digestion stages.

low.restatement: Fingers in the millions, each thin-walled and well drained.
low.analogy: A towel's loops drying far faster than a flat sheet.
low.examPointer: List the villus adaptations; each is a separate mark.

medium.restatement: The design maximises three variables at once: area up, distance down, gradient kept steep by fast drainage.
medium.analogy: A well-designed radiator: many fins, thin metal, strong flow inside.
medium.examPointer: Tie each adaptation to rate — surface, distance, gradient.

glossary.definition: A finger-like projection of the intestinal lining that absorbs digested molecules.
The lymph vessel at each villus's centre that carries fatty acids and glycerol away.
The sub-microscopic surface folds on villus cells that enlarge the absorbing area further.
